claims.text: The local release and selected snapshot place the Garura Parent/Child Tournament source slice in May 1998.
The modeled source slice has two source-pinned card identities: Touch Change! row 042 and Kangaskhan row 043, with source_gap_count 0 for this bounded slice.
The selected lines describe Touch Change! as a participant/Garura Rules-use card and Kangaskhan as a prize for parent/child teams that reached a certain number of wins.
This is a source-pinned promo-family card identity slice, not a complete tournament archive, rules packet, participant ledger, official copy-count source, or marketplace price authority.

Touch Change! carries a reprint caveat: the selected lines and Pokumon note a Pokémon Card Fan Club Vol. 5 insert route in June 1998, so agents must not collapse every Touch Change! copy into the May 1998 tournament route.
The local rows and selected lines credit Nobuyuki Habu for Touch Change! and Ken Sugimori for Kangaskhan, with the credits treated as source/provider metadata rather than physical-card proof.

External artist-index references are useful texture only: The Art of Pokémon lists Nobuyuki Habu with a small Japanese TCG card footprint including Touch Change!, and Ken Sugimori as a major Pokémon/Game Freak art figure with a very large TCG footprint.

The release matters because it makes the Pokemon card game visibly intergenerational: parents and children play as teams, a special rules card teaches the format, and Kangaskhan turns the prize into a perfect family symbol.

Agents should preserve the May 1998 Garura Parent/Child source route, the participation-vs-prize lane, Touch Change! Fan Club reprint caveat, Kangaskhan logo signal, row 042/043 identity, and artist credits before accepting a match.

narrative.human_title: Garura Parent/Child Tournament: the family table becomes a prize lane
narrative.why_it_matters: This is one of those releases where the object only makes full sense when you picture the room. A parent and a child sit together, battle another family pair, and the tournament creates two different kinds of memory: Touch Change! for everyone who needed the Garura Rules machinery, and Kangaskhan for teams that pushed far enough to earn the prize. Kangaskhan is almost too perfect here: a parent Pokemon with its child in the pouch, carrying the emotional thesis of the event. Touch Change! is the quieter marvel, a rules card that proves the tournament format itself became collectible. For an agent, the lesson is not just name matching. The role, route, reprint caveat, and family-tournament context are the identity.

card_highlights.assembly_note: Touch Change! sits in the Garura Parent/Child source slice as row 042; event role and source route need to stay attached to the name.
card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Touch Change! is wonderful because it makes the format itself collectible. It is not the big trophy card, and that is why it matters: it is the little mechanism that let the Parent/Child tournament feel different from normal play. The card says the table has two bodies on each side, two generations leaning over the same game, and a special rule for how they pass the turn between them. Habu’s contribution is gentle and strange: rules text becomes a memory object. The collector trap is the reprint route, because a Touch Change! can belong to the tournament story or to the later Fan Club Vol. 5 magazine route; the agent has to ask which assembly path the seller is actually claiming.

card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Kangaskhan is the emotional center of the release. The tournament asks a parent and child to play as a pair, then rewards successful teams with the Pokémon whose whole design is parenthood made visible. That is why this card has a gravity beyond the checklist row: it is the event’s thesis in one picture. Sugimori’s credit matters because the prize leans on the franchise’s foundational visual language; this does not authenticate any copy, but it explains why the object feels so canonical.
